title: Free or enslaved? Status, experience and memory

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Were Africans in Tudor England free or enslaved? What were their lives like? And did Elizabeth I really try to expel them? This topic weighs the evidence and the interpretations of historians.

blocks.p: English law in the 16th century did not clearly recognise slavery. The evidence suggests most Africans in Tudor England were treated as free people:

ul: They were paid wages (John Blanke, Jacques Francis, Diego).
They were baptised, married and buried in parish churches (Mary Fillis, John Blanke).
They could give evidence in court (Jacques Francis, 1548).

blocks.p: In the 1580s the Portuguese doctor Hector Nunes complained to the Court of Requests that an African man he had bought refused to serve him, and that he had no remedy under English common law. The Pearson GCSE Migrants course uses this petition as evidence about African freedom in Tudor England.

This did not mean equality. Africans usually worked as servants, and words like "blackamoore" could carry negative ideas. At the same time, Englishmen such as John Hawkins began slave-trading voyages from 1562, taking Africans to Spanish America, not England.

sections.title: 2. Experiences of everyday life

blocks.p: Black Tudors worked in many jobs: musicians, divers, sailors, servants, seamstresses and silk weavers. Onyeka argues many were employed for specialist skills; Kaufmann shows them in households from the royal court to villages.
Many were baptised and married English partners, which suggests they were part of local communities rather than separate from them. Others, like Diego, lived mobile lives at sea.
Experiences varied by class, gender, job and place, just as they did for other Tudor people.

evidence: Jobs: musicians, divers, sailors, servants, seamstresses, silk weavers.

blocks.p: On 18 July 1596 the Privy Council issued an open letter allowing Caspar van Senden, a merchant from Lübeck, to take "Blackamoores" from England to Spain and Portugal, but only with their masters' consent.
Masters refused, so van Senden got nothing. A harsher draft proclamation from 1601 survives among Robert Cecil's papers, but it was never issued.

Kaufmann argues this was a failed business deal with one merchant, not a deportation, and Africans stayed in England. The claim that "Elizabeth I expelled all Black people" is a myth that was repeated for years.
How we remember Black Tudors matters. Their stories show that Black British history did not begin in the 20th century.

sources.title: Miranda Kaufmann, "Black Tudors: The Untold Story" (2017)
sources.origin: Written by a historian who researched records such as parish registers, court cases and royal accounts.
sources.purpose: To tell the life stories of ten Africans in Tudor and Stuart England.
sources.usefulness: Built from named individuals in archives. Kaufmann has documented over 360 Africans in Britain between 1500 and 1640. Each life is known only from the records that survive.

sources.title: Onyeka Nubia, "Blackamoores: Africans in Tudor England, their Presence, Status and Origins" (2013)
sources.origin: Written by a British historian after about ten years studying around 250,000 documents.
sources.purpose: To show that Africans were present across Tudor England and to challenge the idea that they were all slaves or outsiders.
sources.usefulness: Argues many Africans had valued skills and that a significant minority were born in England. Like any interpretation, its arguments should be weighed against the evidence.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Africans in Tudor England were free." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh evidence of freedom against evidence of limits and inequality, and reach a judgement.
steps: Evidence of freedom (wages, baptism, court, Nunes).
Evidence of limits (servants, prejudice, slave trade abroad).
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: I largely agree that Africans in Tudor England were free, although they were not treated as equals.
Jacques Francis gave evidence in the High Court of Admiralty in 1548, and in the 1580s Hector Nunes complained that English law gave him no way to force an African man to serve him.
This suggests English law did not enforce slavery, so Africans could work for wages and use the courts; however, most worked as servants and faced prejudiced language such as "blackamoore".
Therefore they were legally free to a large extent, but their freedom had real social limits.
